questions.q: What does an aggregate function do that a row-level function like ISNULL doesn't?
options: Collapses an entire set of rows into a single value
Operates on exactly one row at a time
Can only be used inside a CASE expression
Only works on text columns
questions.explain: Aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, and AVG summarize a whole set of rows into one result.

options: Every row, regardless of NULL values in any column
Only rows where every column is non-NULL
The number of columns in the table
Only distinct rows
questions.explain: COUNT(*) is the 'how many rows total' version — it doesn't look at any specific column's NULL status.

questions.q: Why might COUNT(Color) return a smaller number than COUNT(*) on the same table?
options: COUNT(column) only counts rows where that specific column is not NULL
COUNT(Color) only counts red products
COUNT(*) always returns zero on tables with any NULLs
There is no difference between the two
questions.explain: If some products have no Color recorded (NULL), COUNT(Color) skips those rows while COUNT(*) still counts them.

options: The number of unique, non-NULL color values
The total number of products, regardless of color
The number of NULL color values only
The same thing as COUNT(Color)
questions.explain: DISTINCT combined with COUNT counts each unique value once, rather than counting every occurrence.

questions.q: If 20 products are red, what does COUNT(Color) count them as, versus COUNT(DISTINCT Color)?
options: COUNT(Color) counts all 20 occurrences; COUNT(DISTINCT Color) counts 'Red' once
Both count 'Red' exactly once
Both count all 20 occurrences
COUNT(Color) counts 0, since Color is a text column
questions.explain: This is the core distinction between counting occurrences and counting unique values.
